system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2186-10-13 10:16:00 to 2186-10-15 21:45:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 65-year-old man with recurrent primary central nervous system lymphoma was admitted for his 24th cycle of high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy as part of reinduction therapy. He presented electively in stable condition and received methotrexate 8 g/m² with urinary alkalinization. Temozolomide 240 mg daily was restarted on the same day for a 7-day on/7-day off cycle. Leucovorin rescue was initiated 24 hours post-infusion. Methotrexate levels declined appropriately to 0.13, and he tolerated treatment without complications. Sodium remained stable, and no adjustments were needed to desmopressin. He was discharged home with instructions to continue leucovorin and bicarbonate for 24 hours, resume all home medications, and follow up in clinic for Rituxan and ongoing management.
problems: Primary central nervous system lymphoma, unspecified site, extranodal and solid organ sites
Epilepsy, unspecified, without mention of intractable epilepsy

conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___, one of your care team doctors. You're here today for your high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. My 25th cycle now. I’ve been doing this for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a long journey. I see you’re feeling well today—no fevers, nausea, or headaches?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel okay. Just the usual face numbness. I’ve started using a few drops of medical marijuana elixir to help with that and maybe sleep a bit better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see that noted. Any improvement so far?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not sure yet. It’s only been a few days. I’ll keep trying it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright. We’ll keep an eye on it. Today, we’ll start with IV fluids and sodium bicarbonate to protect your kidneys before the methotrexate infusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, the urine alkalinization. I remember that from last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The goal is to keep your urine less acidic so the methotrexate doesn’t harm your kidneys. We’ll also restart your temozolomide today—240 mg daily for seven days on, seven off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Same as before. And leucovorin starts 24 hours after the chemo, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s correct. It helps ‘rescue’ your healthy cells from the chemo. We’ll monitor your methotrexate levels closely over the next couple of days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Last time, my sodium dropped a bit. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see that in your history. You’re on desmopressin for diabetes insipidus, which can sometimes cause low sodium when combined with IV fluids. But today your sodium is 139, which is normal, so we’ll keep your desmopressin the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I don’t want to feel confused or weak again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring it. Your other labs look stable too—kidney function and liver enzymes are good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my potassium? I think it was low last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was 3.5 this morning—slightly low but not concerning. We’ll keep an eye on it. We can supplement if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to start your methotrexate infusion now—19,440 mg over several hours. You’ll be closely monitored.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I know the drill. Let’s get it done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your methotrexate level came back at 0.61 last night. That’s a good sign—it’s coming down as expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right? No complications so far?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you’re doing well. Your white blood cell count is a bit low at 3.6, but that’s expected with chemo. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had any infections, so that’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll continue your leucovorin and bicarbonate. You’re also due for your next Rituxan clinic visit soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in about a week. I’ve been getting it every three months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—the chemotherapy infusion was completed yesterday, and you’ve tolerated it well so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no side effects. I’m feeling pretty normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest methotrexate level is 0.17, which is excellent. That means it’s almost cleared from your system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you today. You’ll take leucovorin and bicarbonate for one more day at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same doses as in the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly as prescribed. And continue all your regular medications—desmopressin, levetiracetam, sertraline, and the others.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling more down lately. I mentioned that to the nurse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ve scheduled you to see Dr. ___ in the psychiatry clinic. It’s important to address that, especially with everything you’re going through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I appreciate that. And my next MRI is in a month?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to monitor the lymphoma. So far, your treatment is on track. You’ve tolerated this cycle very well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. It’s tough, but I want to keep fighting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Make sure to call if you develop fever, confusion, or any unusual symptoms. Otherwise, follow up with your oncology team as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Everything’s ready for discharge. Your condition is stable, and you’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I’ll take care of myself and see you all next time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers and prescriptions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If your methotrexate level had been higher than 0.2, we’d have kept you longer, but at 0.17, you’re safe to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I was a little nervous about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Completely understandable. But you’ve done well this round.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. One step at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And we’re here to support you every step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doctor. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and rest well at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you next time.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 65-year-old man with recurrent primary central nervous system lymphoma was admitted for his 25th cycle of high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy as part of reinduction therapy. He presented electively in stable condition and received methotrexate 8 g/m² with urinary alkalinization. Temozolomide 240 mg daily was continued on a 7-day on/7-day off cycle. Leucovorin rescue was initiated 24 hours post-infusion. Methotrexate levels declined appropriately to 0.17, and he tolerated treatment without complications. Sodium remained stable, and no adjustments were needed to desmopressin. He reported increased depressive symptoms, prompting a psychiatry clinic referral. He was discharged home with instructions to continue leucovorin and bicarbonate for 24 hours, resume all home medications, and follow up for Rituxan and MRI surveillance in one month.
